Article Title: Two childhood friends who built a $13 million AI startup by age 21 say: Goal was not to build a million-dollar company we did drop out of college for, but to pay for ...
Article Text:
Image credit: X

“The goal wasn't to build a million-dollar company we'd drop out of college for. We just wanted to create something we would find useful, maybe market it a little bit, and if it went well, pay for college with the profits.”

Turbo AI app was built around a problem they faced in college



"We knew AI was good at turning dense text into more digestible formats because we had used it to help us with studying before. So we decided to make a product that combines all of this into a single workflow. Users can either record their lecture or add something they want to study, and we'll use AI to turn it into a variety of aids, such as notes, flashcards, and quiz questions,"

How social media helped the AI startup grow



"I decided to try posting videos about our app three to four times a day on TikTok. Eventually, one video went super viral. I doubled down, more videos took off, and our growth accelerated,"

"My favourite model to use now is Claude Code. A year and a half ago, I started realizing that more of my day-to-day was trying to plan and describe how things are working at a high level and reviewing the AI-generated code than actually writing my own,"

TurboAI founders say they left college after the business gained traction



"We went full-time with our app at the end of our sophomore year, last year. It honestly wasn't a hard decision. Looking back, I think we dropped out a little late. Despite that, I think it can be a big mistake to drop out too early,"

Two childhood friends who built an artificial intelligence (AI) startup that has generated more than $13 million in lifetime revenue by the age of 21 say their original goal was different. The founders of the AI startup said in an interview that their primary aim was not to build a million-dollar company, but to create a product they found useful and earn enough to pay for college.Rudy Arora, co-founder of study app Turbo AI (formerly Turbolearn) told Business Insider,Arora and Sarthak Dhawan, who met in middle school in the suburbs outside Dallas, launched their AI-powered study app in January 2024 after identifying a problem they faced while taking notes during college lectures. At the time, Arora was a freshman at Northwestern University, and Dhawan was studying at Duke University.According to the founders, the app was generating nearly $500,000 in monthly revenue by March 2025. They decided to leave college after completing their sophomore year to focus on the business full-time.The founders said the idea came from their own experience of struggling to listen to lectures while taking notes.Arora said.Before starting the AI app, the pair had worked on other projects in high school, including a marketplace connecting customers with Christmas light installers and a grade-checking application. They said those ventures helped them understand product development and customer feedback, even though both businesses were eventually discontinued.The founders initially promoted the app by approaching students on campus before shifting their focus to TikTok.Arora noted.As demand increased, the company expanded its marketing strategy by hiring creators to post videos about the app. The founders also said AI tools have significantly changed their software development process.Dhawan added.The company now has 10 full-time employees, including six engineers, and has crossed $13 million in lifetime revenue, according to the founders.The founders said they chose to drop out only after the company had established a sustainable business.Arora highlighted. He also cautioned against leaving college before a business has demonstrated meaningful progress."Still, I would caution against dropping out without any real payoff. I see way too many people dropping out with only an idea or at a very early stage of building," Arora warned.
Article Summary: Two childhood friends built an artificial intelligence (AI) startup that has generated more than $13 million in lifetime revenue by the age of 21. Rudy Arora and Sarthak Dhawan, who met in middle school in the suburbs outside Dallas, launched their AI-powered study app in January 2024. They decided to leave college after completing their sophomore year to focus on the business full- time.

Article Title: Jio Haptik launches Solo AI team to help India's entrepreneurs and small businesses grow faster
Article Text:
What Jio Haptik Solo will offer its customers



“We believe accessible AI and AI Teams can change that equation at scale. Just as affordable digital connectivity unlocked unprecedented entrepreneurial opportunities over the past decade, AI Teams will be the next big technological shift to power India's small-business economy. With Solo, we are putting an intelligent growth team in the hands of every entrepreneur - one that works around the clock to help them compete, grow and build with confidence. Our ambition is to empower more than two million solopreneurs and small businesses over the next three years.”

Jio Haptik Solo is built using insights from small and medium-sized businesses



Jio Haptik has launched Solo, an AI-native platform designed to help entrepreneurs and small businesses automate marketing, sales and customer support tasks. The Reliance Jio-backed conversational AI company said the platform aims to make AI-powered business tools accessible to entrepreneurs with limited resources and plans to reach more than two million solopreneurs and small businesses over the next three years. The company said Solo is available on Android and iOS with a free plan, while paid plans start at Rs 2,000 per month.According to Jio Haptik, the platform is built for businesses that primarily operate through channels such as Instagram and WhatsApp, including home-based businesses, boutiques, clinics, salons, freelancers and direct-to-consumer (D2C) sellers. It is designed to automate tasks including content creation, customer engagement, lead generation, sales and customer support.Unlike conventional AI assistants that respond only when prompted, Jio Haptik says Solo functions as an autonomous AI business team. The platform includes two AI teammates: Tara, who handles marketing activities, and Ved, who manages sales and customer support.The company said users can get started by connecting their website or Instagram page, or by uploading a product image. Solo then analyses the business and automatically creates marketing plans, generates social media content, produces product images and videos, runs advertisements, responds to customer queries on WhatsApp and follows up with potential customers.Business owners can review and approve actions before they are carried out.Speaking about the launch, Ahshad Jussawala, Jio Haptik CEO, said,Jio Haptik said Solo was developed using insights from hundreds of solopreneurs and learnings from Interakt's customer base of more than 100,000 small and medium businesses. The company added that over 10,000 businesses have already joined the platform during its early access phase.Saumil Shah, Jio Haptik CTO, said, “The evolution of AI isn't about building better agents; it's about building systems that can take ownership of meaningful work. With Solo, we've combined autonomous planning, execution, and continuous learning into an AI business team designed specifically for entrepreneurs. Tara and Ved don't just respond to prompts; they understand business context, coordinate work across marketing, sales, and customer support, and continuously work towards measurable outcomes. We believe this shift from AI agents to AI teammates will redefine how millions of businesses operate over the coming decade.”Jio Haptik also provided customer feedback from early users, such as Hirdyesh Mordani, a home baker, who stated that the platform enabled business operations instantly after linking to the Instagram page and adding product photos.According to the company, Solo is part of its broader effort to expand AI adoption among India's micro, small and medium enterprises by offering automation tools that require minimal technical expertise.
Article Summary: Jio Haptik has launched Solo, an AI-native platform designed to help entrepreneurs and small businesses automate marketing, sales and customer support tasks. Article Title: Global head of macro research at Germany's largest bank Deutsche Bank says: My view on AI and jobs is slightly skewed by what economic history tells us, as at every point ...
Article Text:
Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid on AI and jobs



AI productivity gains will take time

AI boom raises market questions

AI will significantly improve productivity, but its biggest impact on economies may still take years to materialise, according to Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Germany's largest bank, Deutsche Bank. In an interview with Bloomberg Television, Reid said history makes him optimistic about AI's effect on jobs despite growing concerns over automation. He argued that every major technological breakthrough has raised fears about job losses, but those concerns have not been realised on a broad scale. Reid also said businesses will need time to fully integrate AI before its productivity benefits become clear.Reid said his view on AI is shaped by economic history rather than short-term fears. “My view on AI and jobs is slightly skewed by what economic history tells us,” he said. “At every point of a new breakthrough in innovation, we've been really scared about jobs, about new technology destroying jobs, and it has never happened in aggregate.”According to a Bloomberg report, Reid believes AI will ultimately create jobs and improve productivity over the long term.Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid said AI has greater productivity potential than any technology he has seen during his career.“In my career I haven't seen anything like AI in terms of potential for productivity,” he said. “But I would probably caution that going to take a number of years for us to properly embed it into enterprises to really get the benefits of that.”He said companies will need time to integrate AI into everyday operations before seeing its full economic impact.According to the Bloomberg report, investors are closely watching the rapid rise in semiconductor stocks and growing spending on AI infrastructure. Some policymakers have questioned whether the market is entering an AI bubble.Acknowledging the risk, Reid said: “There's a risk obviously, when you see parabolic rises up, that at some point there's a big tech bust.”Despite concerns over AI valuations, Reid pointed to centuries of technological progress. “But I would kind of go back to the fact that humans have been innovating for 250, 300 years since the Industrial Revolution,” he said. "We've been fantastic at innovating in that quarter of a millennium. We've only seen inflation go up."
Article Summary: Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid said AI has greater productivity potential than any technology he has seen during his career. Reid said companies will need time to integrate AI into everyday operations before seeing its full economic impact. Some policymakers have questioned whether the market is entering an AI bubble.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Elon Musk: "Some people don't like change, but you need to embrace change if…"
Article Text:
Elon Musk

Quote of the day by Elon Musk

What Elon Musk means by embracing change

How Tesla and SpaceX prove the point

When change is not actually worth it

A simple test before you resist change

What Elon Musk’s career actually shows

Other famous quotes by Elon Musk

"When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favor."

"Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough."

"I'd rather be optimistic and wrong than pessimistic and right."

"It's very important to have a feedback loop, where you're constantly thinking about what you've done and how you could be doing it better."

Nobody enjoys change much. Most people put up with it only when they have to, and avoid it whenever they can get away with staying the same. Elon Musk pushes back on that instinct with a simple line: "Some people don't like change, but you need to embrace change if the alternative is disaster." His point isn't that change is fun. It's that the real comparison isn't between change and comfort. It's between change and whatever happens if nothing changes at all."Some people don't like change, but you need to embrace change if the alternative is disaster."A lot of people treat "things staying the same" as the safe option by default, just because it's familiar. Musk's quote pushes back on that assumption directly. Staying the same only feels safe. Whether it actually is safe depends entirely on where the current path is heading. If it's heading toward failure anyway, resisting change isn't caution. It's just a slower way of arriving at the same bad outcome.Tesla is a good example of this in practice. Scaling up to mass-produce the Model 3 meant throwing out a lot of familiar car manufacturing methods and betting heavily on automation that, at first, caused real problems on the production line.The comfortable choice would have been to stay small and stick with methods that already worked. Musk pushed through the mess instead, and Tesla eventually hit production numbers nobody expected from it.SpaceX did something similar with reusable rockets. The rest of the aerospace industry had mostly written the idea off as impractical. Early tests failed, expensively and publicly. Instead of dropping the idea, SpaceX kept iterating until reusable boosters became normal, and launch costs dropped in a way the old approach never would have allowed.This isn't a blanket argument for change just for the sake of it. Change adopted because it's trendy or new can cause just as much damage as stubbornly refusing to change at all. The real question Musk's quote is pointing at is narrower: is the current path actually heading somewhere bad. If yes, change is worth the mess it creates. If not, there's no reason to disrupt something that's working fine.Most people don't run rocket companies, but the same test works at a much smaller scale. If a job, a routine, or a relationship has started quietly declining, the question isn't whether changing it feels uncomfortable. It's what things will actually look like in a year or two if nothing changes.A simple way to check this is to say out loud, specifically, what happens if you do nothing. Not a vague feeling of unease, an actual guess at the outcome. Vague discomfort is easy to sit with forever. A clear, named consequence is much harder to keep ignoring.Musk's quote isn't really about loving change. It's about being honest with yourself about where staying the same is actually taking you. Several of his companies were built on exactly that kind of honesty, made at moments when the easier, more comfortable choice was sitting right there waiting to be taken.
Article Summary: Elon Musk's quote of the day: "Some people don't like change, but you need to embrace change if the alternative is disaster" Staying the same only feels safe. Whether it actually is safe depends entirely on where the current path is heading.
